tables.description: Comparative analysis of lighting effects on human well-being and performance from different studies, including study objectives, methodology, and major findings related to lighting.

limitations: Sample sizes of reviewed studies were small and often limited to a single group, making generalization difficult.
Some reviewed studies (e.g., Kazemi et al. [11]) found it challenging to generalize results beyond specific populations (e.g., postgraduate students).
Reviewed studies (e.g., Kim et al. [12], Sun et al. [20]) often studied small numbers of occupants (e.g., 10 occupants, young college students), limiting applicability to general office workers.
Issues with evaluation methods and data analysis were noted in some reviewed studies (e.g., Deng et al. [5] used Digital ID for indoor comfort, raising privacy concerns).
Some reviewed studies (e.g., Lee and Kim [14]) did not account for temporal variables (e.g., morning/afternoon) that could affect working memory.
Some reviewed studies (e.g., Katabaro and Yan [10]) did not clearly distinguish between sunlight and artificial light during illuminance measurements.
Further research is required on the impact of lighting glare and colour rendering on human behaviour, which has not been studied deeply in most research, affecting visual performance and comfort.
Gaps in participant diversity, evaluation methods, and data analysis persist across the reviewed literature.
Ethical considerations and experimental design issues also need addressing in future research.

The scope of this systematic review was limited to peer-reviewed articles from a single database (Scopus), potentially excluding other academic work (e.g., dissertations, research reports) and more extensive results from specialized databases (e.g., Web of Science, PsycINFO, PubMed).
